newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's West Coast suffers rare, harsh blizzard.
newsitem.headline: Canada's West Coast suffers rare, harsh blizzard.

text.p: British Columbia, known more for its temperate winters while the rest of Canada suffers through Arctic blasts, was shoveling itself out on Monday from its worst blizzard in decades.

The snowstorm dumped 27 inches (70 cm) on the province's capital, Victoria, and 18 inches (45 cm) on its largest city, Vancouver, over the weekend, paralysing public transportation and stretching the capacity of the few snowplows to the limit.
Vancouver awoke to its more usual rain on Monday morning, allowing most buses to resume operation, but freezing rain throughout Sunday night added to the headaches facing ploughs and emergency crews.
"We're so unequipped for snow, especially to this extent," said Victoria-based Sarah Booker of British Columbia's emergency programme.
"Our emergency vehicles had enough troubles with soft snow, let alone when it gets ice on top of it. That sort of compounds it for us."
Many in the rest of Canada could barely contain their glee.

"Revenge is sweet," triumphed a headline in the Citizen of Ottawa newspaper. Ottawa had seven feet (1.8 metres) of snow by Christmas, 1995 but this year has only had a few inches while enjoying unseasonable warmth.

"While the rest of the country is usually buried in snow and suffering through -40 temperatures Fahrenheit (-40 Celsius), Vancouverites are often out on the golf courses. Well, the fates have briefly changed," the normally staid newspaper wrote.

Some British Columbians made the most of the weekend weather, cross-country skiing through city streets or Vancouver's Stanley Park, while others donned wetsuits to surf 30-foot (10-metre) waves off Vancouver Island's west coast.
But Vancouver International Airport operated at only 10 percent capacity on Sunday and was struggling to get planes moving on Monday.
"Some of those aircraft are absolutely coated in ice from (freezing rain during) the night and from the snow yesterday that hasn't melted," airport operations official Danielle Moore said.

Canadian National Railway trains were at a standstill, reported the Canadian Wheat Board, which sends most of its grain by train to the Vancouver port. However, the board had enough stocks already at the port to continue shipping.
